title: How Tourette Syndrome Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Tourette syndrome: its naming after French physician Georges Gilles de la Tourette (with Jean Marc Gaspard Itard credited as an earlier describer), onset in childhood, genetic and dopamine theories, brain regions suspected, simple and complex motor and vocal tics, coprolalia and other rarer tic types, diagnostic criteria, tics spreading down the body, links to OCD and ADHD, treatments from habit reversal therapy to antipsychotics and experimental deep brain stimulation, famous people with Tourette's, and a listener mail about patriot offsets.

segments.title: Opening banter and Bob Saget YouTube Tourette's
segments.summary: Hosts open with casual banter about the studio and then discuss a YouTube personality whose outbursts are often assumed to be Tourette's, and whether he actually has the condition.

segments.title: Naming and history of Tourette syndrome
segments.summary: The hosts explain the spelling of Tourette syndrome and its name origin. Jean Marc Gaspard Itard described an elderly noblewoman with the symptoms first, and Gilles de la Tourette later published on nine patients in a French hospital, leading to the name.

segments.title: Onset, age, and genetics
segments.summary: Tourette's usually begins before age eighteen, often around age seven with a peak between eight and twelve, then tics decline. Boys are affected more than girls. A parent with Tourette's has about a fifty percent chance of passing it on, which supports a genetic basis, though no gene has been identified.

segments.title: Coprolalia and other tic types
segments.summary: The hosts describe coprolalia, the involuntary blurting of obscenities, and note it occurs in a minority of sufferers, with ways people mask it. They discuss a related sub-symptom of blurting slurs and the prevalence of mild cases compared with severe cases in the US, and cultural differences.

segments.title: Brain research and dopamine theory
segments.summary: Researchers have narrowed candidate brain regions to the thalamus, basal ganglia, and frontal cortex. The hosts consider this weak. The leading theory is dopamine misfiring, inferred from Parkinson's disease, where dopamine is lacking.

segments.title: Tic symptoms, diagnosis, and classification
segments.summary: Common tics include eye blinking, throat clearing, and shoulder shrugging. Diagnosis requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic within a year, after other causes are ruled out. Tourette's falls under movement disorders. Tics often start high in the body and move downward with age, and can build up as an urge that is relieved by ticking.

segments.title: Treatments, associated disorders, and famous people
segments.summary: Habit reversal therapy uses a competing response, and cognitive behavioral therapy addresses stress. Drugs such as antipsychotics are reserved for severe cases due to side effects. Tourette's often co-occurs with OCD and ADHD. Experimental deep brain stimulation is mentioned. Famous people with Tourette's or related tics are named, and the hosts cover other tic types and medical marijuana research.

segments.title: Listener mail: Patriot offsets
segments.summary: A listener named Rob compares carbon offsets to Catholic indulgences and jokingly offers the hosts military service years as patriot offsets. The hosts respond and mention a Civil War conscription substitution practice.
